description: Top speed is not mostly muscle. It is a sling at the front of your hip, snapping your leg through faster than effort ever could. Today you swing at full speed against the clock, learn why sprinters are built on hip tendons, and measure the sling you already own.

lines: The count ends when form does.
beats.title: SPEED WITH A FULL ARC

scenes.narration: Stand sideways at a wall, one hand resting on it for balance. This time the swing is not relaxed. Swing the outside leg forward and back as fast as you can, through the fullest arc you can control, tall through the body, no leaning, no hopping on the standing leg. Twenty seconds. Count every full swing, forward and back counting as one, until the speed or the arc starts to die. Then turn around and do the other leg. Two numbers, smaller one is the truth. Write it down. At the end of this video I will tell you what this frantic little test reveals about the fastest tissue in your body, and why the quickest men alive are built exactly like you.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN SLOW AND SNAPPY
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twenty-two full-speed swings in twenty seconds is where a sleepy hip becomes a snappy one. Under seventeen, your hip sling is returning the leg so slowly that your muscles have to drag it through, which is why your top speed feels like hard work. Over thirty, you own the leg speed of a sprinter's warm-up drill, the kind coaches film in slow motion and study. Notice that this test cannot be passed by being strong. A powerful but slow hip scores terribly. The only way to swing fast is to let the tendons do what they evolved to do, and that is exactly what we are grading.
scenes.sub: under 17: muscles dragging the leg - over 30: sprinter territory

lines: Stretched at the back of the stride,
it snaps the leg forward free.
beats.title: HOW THE SLING WORKS

scenes.narration: Watch a sprinter in slow motion and look at the recovery leg, the one swinging forward after push-off. It folds and whips through at a speed no muscle can produce by contracting. Muscles are simply too slow. The speed comes from a sling. As the leg reaches the back of the stride, the hip flexor tendon and the tissues around the front of the hip are stretched tight. Then, like a drawn catapult releasing, they snap the leg forward, and the muscle's job is mostly to guide the flight and prepare the landing. Sports scientists call this elastic recoil, and at top speed it does the majority of the work of leg recovery. This is the great secret of fast men. They are not pulling their legs forward harder than you. Their slings are snapping the leg forward for them. Your swing test measures that snap with a wall and a stopwatch. A high count means the sling stretches fully and releases fast. A low count means the leg is being dragged by effort, and effort has a speed limit that elastic tissue simply does not.

beats.text: THE STANDING LEG IS HALF THE TEST

scenes.narration: Here is what your two numbers are really telling you. A fast swing needs two hips doing opposite jobs. The swinging side provides the sling. The standing side provides the platform, and its tendons, the glute attachments on the outside of the hip, have to hold your pelvis level while the other leg whips. If the platform sways, the sling cannot release at full speed, because the body will not let it. This is why we always grade both sides. The slower side is not always the worse sling. Sometimes it is the better sling standing on the worse platform. The test cannot tell you which, and it does not need to. Training both sides, swings and stance work together, fixes both. Sprint coaches have known this forever. It is why their athletes do as much single-leg stability work as speed work. The ceiling on your speed is set by the side you would rather not test, which is precisely why we test it.

lines: and what cannot stretch cannot snap.
beats.title: LENGTH BEFORE SPEED

scenes.narration: One warning before we train, because it decides whether your speed work works. A sling can only snap as far as it can stretch. If your hip flexor tendon has adapted to the short position of a chair, the back of your stride is cut off early, and the catapult starts its release half-drawn. This is why so many desk workers feel slow in a way they cannot explain. Their muscles are fine. Their slings have been shortened by furniture. The relaxed swinging from our earlier hip work is the maintenance that keeps the sling long. The fast swinging in this video is the training that teaches it to release. You need both, in that order. Length before speed, always. A short, fast sling is an injury looking for a date. A long, fast sling is a sprinter. The difference between them is about two minutes of daily swinging, which might be the best trade in this entire series.

beats.text: FAST LEGS LIVE ON LIGHT FRAMES

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage, and in this test it is almost unfair. The sling has to swing your leg, and your leg is the lightest load a hip can be asked to cycle. Heavy men swing heavy pendulums. Their slings work harder for fewer cycles, and their counts show it. The history of sprinting is a parade of lean frames for a reason that has nothing to do with fashion. Less mass on the pendulum means a faster cycle rate, and cycle rate is top speed. You were issued the sprinter's chassis at birth. The only question this test asks is whether the sling attached to it has ever been trained. Twenty seconds will tell us.

Now we teach the sling to snap together. Hand on the wall, tall body, full-speed swings. Twenty seconds, rest, switch sides. Four rounds, two per leg. Full arc or it does not count. When the arc shrinks, the set is over. Swing. Go.

beats.text: RELAXED DAILY, FAST TWICE A WEEK
CHASING SPEED ON A SHORT SLING

scenes.narration: Here is your week. Relaxed swings daily to keep the sling long, fast swings twice a week to teach it violence, and single-leg balance work on the days between. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: chasing speed on a short sling. If the front of your hip pulls tight and dull during fast work, go back to relaxed swinging for a week. Length is the foundation and it is not negotiable. Mistake two: leaning back to fake a bigger arc. The wall hand is for balance, not for gymnastics. Stay tall or the count is fiction. Mistake three: holding your breath and bracing. A sling releases from a relaxed body. Tension is the brake you are trying to remove. One extra full-speed swing a week is the pace. In half a year, that is a different gear you did not have, installed in the fastest tissue you own.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME WALL, FULL ARC
scenes.narration: So, your number, grading the smaller side as always. Under seventeen: your legs are being dragged through every stride by muscle, and your top speed has been paying for it. Seventeen to twenty-two: the sling is engaging, the snap is arriving. Over twenty-two: fast hips, recycling energy like the system was designed to. Over thirty: sprinter territory, and your warm-up drill looks like other men's main event. Put the smaller number in the comments. Just the swings. In thirty days we swing at full speed again.
scenes.sub: comment your smaller number - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now we swing again at full speed, and the sling will report what a month of snapping taught it. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave the smaller number in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Leg Swing Test Reveals Your Hidden Strength
